notes: TBox rule edit. Derivability very_unlikely: see evidence. Two determinate queries on new members named in the prompt (the rule is the only route) and two background-belief queries on well-known members whose value a model may store by name. In a world where the stored value wins, the member's class membership gives way (with the side facts listed in the world); it never stays in the class as an exception to the edited rule. The two members' storage choices are independent, so four worlds. R1: no snake eats plants; egg-, snail-, insect- and worm-eaters all count as carnivorous ('strictly carnivorous', Wikipedia). 'Carnivorous' is used, not 'carnivore', to avoid the order Carnivora. Well-known members: the boa constrictor and pythons, chosen because their names do not contain 'snake' and their diet is stated by name ('pythons are carnivores' 280; 'boa constrictor AND carnivorous' 132; boa diet of rodents 626). Avoided king cobra, anaconda and black mamba, whose superlatives ('longest venomous snake', 'heaviest snake') entail their snake membership. Pythons leaving the snake class has one side fact (the reticulated python stops being the longest snake), which is about the member itself, not a firm fact outside the chain; kept, as the ostrich in 0006. New members are named in the prompt with membership stated; the prompts give no habitat or prey hint. Near query asks a different relation of the same class (reptile), whose answer differs from 'herbivorous'. Verifier: snake frugivory is anecdotal only (fruit found in a black-necked spitting cobra and an Indian rock python, the latter fruit carrying insect larvae); no snake takes a meaningful share of its diet from plants, so the rule has no real exception.
